JUDGMENT DELIVERED:

THOMSON
J.

INTRODUCTION/BACKGROUND

[
1
]

Following a
lengthy trial before a different judge of this court, a final order was
pronounced on July 30, 2007. (See:
Shore-Kalo v. Kalo
,
2007 MBQB
197 (CanLII)
.)

[
2
]

That order
addresses a number of issues between the parties, including custody of their
two children. The petitioner is granted sole custody of the children, and significant
limits on the respondent’s access to the children are put into place.

[
3
]

The focus of this
court’s attention in the current proceeding relates to those terms of the final
order, which provide relief to the petitioner, made pursuant to
The

Domestic Violence and Stalking Act
, C.C.S.M. c. D93 (the “
DSVA
”).

[
4
]

Those provisions made
pursuant to the
DSVA
enjoin the respondent from following the
petitioner and/or either of the children “from place to place at any time other
than during his periods of supervised access”, and also limits and/or
proscribes his communication with them, and his attendance or entry at any
place where they reside or attend. The relief granted is a “prevention order”
pursuant to
s. 14(1)
of the
DSVA
.

[
5
]

The terms of the
final order, concerning the respondent’s access, were previously varied by the
trial judge on August 4, 2009, to expand the respondent’s time with the
children. The prevention order (contained in the final order) was also varied
to facilitate or permit that added contact. (See:
Shore-Kalo v. Kalo
,

2009 MBQB 209 (CanLII)
)

[
6
]

The current
proceeding was brought by the respondent through his filing of a further notice
of motion to vary the final order, in which he requests revocation of the prevention
order in its entirety, as it pertains to both the petitioner and the children.

THE PARTIES’ POSITIONS/EVIDENCE

[
7
]

Since filing, the
respondent has refined his position, and the petitioner has agreed to some of
the relief sought. The respondent has withdrawn his request to revoke the
prevention order, or to vary the terms of that order, as they relate to the
petitioner. The petitioner has agreed to deletion of those terms of the
prevention order relating to the respondent’s attendance at the Jewish
Community Centre and at the Shaarey Zedek Synagogue.

[
8
]

The respondent’s
discrete remaining request, to which these reasons for decision now apply, is
to delete or to vary those provisions of the prevention order obtained by the petitioner,
which limit or proscribe his contact with his two children, such that there are
no restrictions whatsoever upon him.

[
9
]

The respondent’s
motion was filed together with his affidavit affirmed on August 1, 2018.

[
10
]

The petitioner filed an affidavit (affirmed
September 14, 2018), and affidavits deposed by each of the now adult children (both
deposed on that same date). The respondent filed a second affidavit, affirmed
September 21, 2018.

[
11
]

No cross-examinations have been
conducted.

[
12
]

At the direction of the court early
in the proceedings, the children were given notice of the proceedings, although
they are not “parties”. They appeared together before me at the hearing of the
motion.

[
13
]

Emily Caitlin Kalo is a university student.
Several months before her 18
th
birthday in October of last year, she
terminated all contact with the respondent. Her evidence is that she did so
because of the respondent’s aggressive, mean and emotionally abusive conduct
towards her. He has ignored her requests that he cease initiating contact with
her, resulting in extreme emotional upset to her. He attended her convocation
in May 2018 and behaved in a manner (“arguing with other parents, standing
up and moving around the sanctuary, speaking loudly, sitting in the front row
reserved for teaching staff, and mocking students as they were receiving their
awards”) which caused her to weep throughout the ceremony. She also indicates
she is frightened by him, and does not want him attending her home, place of
schooling or place of employment.

[
14
]

Stephanie Kalo is a year older than
her sister. She, too, is a university student. Unlike her sister, she continues
to have ongoing contact with the respondent, at times and locations as she
chooses. She describes his behavior during visits as “often erratic and
unpredictable”, and that he is “not able to manage his temper”. She also
indicates she is frightened by him, and does not want him attending her home,
place of schooling or place of employment.

[
15
]

At the hearing of the motion, they
both addressed the court indicating that, consistent with their affidavit
evidence, they continued to be fearful of the respondent.  While not concerned
that he would inflict physical harm, it seems clear they fear emotional or
psychological harm from his contact with them and/or that he will “stalk” them in
the absence of the prevention order
.

[
16
]

The contents of the respondent’s
affidavits (one deposed before his receipt of his daughters’ affidavits, and
the other subsequent) cover a broad array of matters. The following provides a
sufficient summary:

•

he improperly
discloses information contained in the petitioner’s case management information
statement;

•

he attaches as an
exhibit his “Jewish Community membership card”;

•

he makes legal
arguments as to “the scope of the prevention order” (it contains “harsh and
far-reaching restrictions”) and to his children being adults, and no longer
being “under the care and control of the petitioner”, making the prevention
order “outdated and anachronistic”;

•

he references his
having “been in the news a few times, recently, in the context of high profile
litigation involving me”;

•

he speaks of
compliments he received at his daughter’s convocation from “a retired Judge of
the Court of Appeal”, but denies seeing his younger daughter crying during the
ceremony, at which she was the valedictorian; and,

•

he generally
denies engaging in any inappropriate or objectionable contact or communications
with his daughters, at any time.

THE LAW

[
17
]

The original request of the court for
the limits upon or proscription of the respondent’s contact or communication
with the petitioner and with the parties’ children was made, and an order
obtained, by the petitioner on her own behalf and on behalf of her children.

[
18
]

While there are no explicit provisions
in the
DSVA

specific to applications by an adult person on behalf
of their minor child (for either a protection order or a prevention order), I
note the definition of a “specified person” at
s. 1(1)
, and also the wording of

ss. 2(2)
and
2(3)
(d), and also reference ss. 7(1) and (2) of the Regulation
117/99, made under the
DSVA
, as follows:

Definition

1(1)

"specified person"
includes a person who is a
member of a group of persons specified in a protection order or prevention
order;

Meaning
of “stalking”

2(2)
Stalking occurs when a
person, without lawful excuse or authority and knowing that another person is
harassed or recklessly as to whether the other person is harassed, repeatedly
engages in conduct that causes the other person reasonably, in all the circumstances,
to fear for his or her own safety.

Examples of conduct

2(3)
The
conduct referred to in subsection (2) includes the person

…..

(d)   engaging in threatening conduct directed at the other
person or anyone known to the other person.

Application
on behalf of a minor

7(1) If
the subject is a minor, an adult person may make an application on behalf of
the subject.

Evidence
required to support application

7(2)

An
application made under subsection (1) must be supported by sworn document or sworn
testimony that sets out the following, in addition to the requirements of subsection
3(1):

(a)   the subject's date of birth;

(b)   the name of the person making the application,
and his or her relationship to the subject;

(c)    the consent of the person making the application
to act on behalf of the subject;

(d)   a statement that the person making the
application has no interest adverse to that of the subject;

(e)   a statement that the person making the
application is aware that he or she could be required to pay personally any
costs awarded against the person or the subject.

[
19
]

The request now
made of the respondent engages
s. 19(1)
of the
DSVA
, which
specifies the “test” for deletion or variation of any term or condition in a
prevention order, or for revocation of the order:

Court may vary or revoke order

19(1)
The court, on application at any time after a protection order
is filed in the court under subsection 10(2) or a prevention order is made
under subsection 14(1), may, if satisfied that it is fit and just to do
so,

(a)

delete or vary any term or condition in the order, or add terms
and conditions, which may include any provision mentioned in
clauses 14(1)(a) to (p); or

(b)

revoke the order.

[
20
]

The respondent has filed a pleading
in the form of a notice of motion to vary a final order (which, in the normal
course, would engage the court in consideration of the threshold issue, namely,
whether there has been a material change in circumstances since the final order
was pronounced).  I choose to consider the matter procedurally as an
application to delete or vary under s. 19(1) of the
DVSA
, and
that no material change in circumstances need be established (see:
T.L.L.
v. J.J.L
.,
2015 MBCA 68
(Can LII) at para.
17
).

ANALYSIS AND DECISION

[
21
]

The legislation does not, in my view,
admit of a resolution of the issue before the court upon the basis of the
children “aging out” of the prevention order upon attaining the age of majority,
or the order otherwise “lapsing” in tandem with the custody and access terms of
the final order, both suggestions made by the respondent.

[
22
]

While it may be correct that the
custody and access provisions of the final order are no longer operative or of
application because the children are now adults, it does not follow that the
prevention order as it pertains to them is no longer in place. The fate of the
prevention order is not, in my view, entwined with, or dependent upon, the
custody order.

[
23
]

First, the terms of
the final order, which address custody and access, were made under separate,
federal legislation, the
Divorce Act
, R.S.C., 1985, c. 3 (2
nd

Supp.).
The
prevention order was pronounced pursuant the
DSVA
, and our Court
of Appeal has stated that, “the ‘pith and substance’ of this Act is in the nature
of crime prevention
and thus falls under provincial jurisdiction
” (
Baril v.
Obelnicki
,
2007 MBCA 40 (CanLII)
,
at para.
3
).

[
24
]

Our Court of Appeal
has also made clear that, unlike a protection order granted under the
DSVA
,

a prevention order admits of no specified time period of application,
and remains in place indefinitely,
pending further court order.  “
Once
the order has been made, served on the responding party, and filed in court,
the order remains in effect until a judge is satisfied on application “that it
is fit and just” (at
section 19(1)
)
to vary or revoke the order.” (
R. v. Dilk
,
2016 MBCA 98 (CanLII)
,
at para.
14
).

[
25
]

The question, then, is whether it is
fit and just to do so, in the present case.

[
26
]

A determination as to whether it is
“fit and just” to delete or vary the terms of a prevention order of course requires
some contextual analysis. This may be pursued here by a focused consideration
of the pertinent legislation, and its intent; a review of the findings made by
the trial judge in connection with the prevention order she pronounced; and, my
consideration of, in the context of those reasons, the recent evidence
submitted by the parties (referenced in part, above, at paras. 13 to 16).

[
27
]

The
Baril

decision
sets
out the social context background to and the purpose of the
DSVA
:

6
The

Act
came into force in 1999.  It was designed to address a pressing
concern in Manitoba – violence in the area of domestic violence and
stalking.  See Dorothy Pedlar, Commissioner,
The Domestic Violence
Review into the Administration of Justice in Manitoba
(August 1991) (the
Pedlar
Report
), The Honourable Mr. Justice Perry W. Schulman, Commissioner,
A
Study of Domestic Violence and the Justice System in Manitoba
(June 1997)
(the
Lavoie Inquiry
), and Manitoba Law Reform Commission,
Stalking
,
Report #98 (May 1997) (the
Report on Stalking
).

7
The

Act
created two different types of orders – protection orders, obtained
from a designated justice of the peace of the Provincial Court of Manitoba, and
prevention orders, obtained from the Court of Queen’s Bench.

…..

9
These protection orders may contain
a variety of provisions, ranging from prohibiting the respondent from attending
at the applicant’s residence or place of employment to peace officer assistance
in removing the respondent from premises.  The provisions do not contain
the more powerful remedies available in a prevention order from a judge of the
Court of Queen’s Bench, such as sole occupation of the family residence or
payment of compensation for monetary losses due to domestic violence or
stalking.

…..

82
Violence
in human relationships has become an issue of public concern in Manitoba during
recent years.  The concern has focused on two specific types of violence –
domestic violence and stalking.  In the case of stalking, there exists an
extensive literature on the dynamics of stalking, its overpowering impact on
the victim, usually a woman, and the necessity for the law to assist the
stalking victim to sever her interaction with the stalker in order to protect
herself.  There is a significant power imbalance between the perpetrators
and victims of stalking and that power imbalance holds the potential for tragic
consequences in the absence of timely intervention.  See, for example,
Karen M. Abrams & Gail Erlick Robinson, “Stalking Part I:  An Overview
of the Problem” (1998), 43 Can. J. Psychiatry 473, and “Stalking Part II:
Victims’ Problems With the Legal System and Therapeutic Considerations” (1998),
43 Can. J. Psychiatry 477.

83
The
Manitoba Law Reform Commission described the obsessive conduct that the stalker
directs towards the victim and the sometimes devastating effect on the
victim.  As it concluded in its
Report on Stalking
(at p. 52):

Stalking is
a serious problem in Manitoba, especially for women.  As discussed in
Chapter 1, stalkers can have a devastating effect on the lives of those who are
stalked, subjecting them to harassment and fear in their homes, at work and in
public places for months or even years.  Those who are stalked often feel
that they have lost control of their lives and in many cases are helpless to do
anything to remedy the situation.

84
It
found that Manitoba law was inadequate to provide private recourse for
stalking.  In terms of prevention, the Commission concluded that “[t]he
principal need” of the subject of stalking was a legal regime to ensure “that
the stalking end and that the subject be left alone” (at p. 27) and that
“[e]xperts agree that perhaps the most effective means of preventing stalking
is early intervention.  If the courts are properly engaged in a stalking
situation before it escalates into violence, many of the tragedies resulting
from stalking can be avoided” (at p. 53).

[
28
]

The trial proceeded over the course
of many weeks in 2007.  The respondent was self-represented throughout. The
opportunity available to the trial judge to observe and assess the respondent,
and his history of conduct, was broad and deep. I refer to the following
portions of Allen J.’s reasons for decision in
Shore-Kalo
2007,
particularly addressing the issue of the requested prevention order:

[120]  In September 2004,
the court granted, on an interim basis, a prevention order under the
DVSA
.  The order basically prevented the
husband from following, contacting or communicating with the wife and
children.  He was not allowed to attend or enter anywhere they resided or
regularly attended, including the daycare, school, grandparents’ home and the
places of the children’s extra curricular activities while those activities
were on.  The husband was also ordered to see a psychiatrist.

[121]  As the husband’s
behaviour became more and more outrageous, the wife returned to court for more
protection.  In June 2005, as a result of the husband’s picketing and
behaviour at the synagogue, the court set out a perimeter boundary around the
Asper Campus where the children attended daycare and school and ordered that
the husband not attend the synagogue if the wife notified him that she and the
children were going to be there.

[122]  However, these
restraints only appeared to whet the husband’s imagination in terms of what to
do next in his battles with the wife’s family and the Jewish community.
During the period of time that JCFS was supervising his visits, he began
trolling through court files to see what information he could find and use
against those who he perceived to be his enemies.  As mentioned earlier,
he circulated portions of an affidavit filed by a daycare worker in her
domestic litigation.  He sent cryptic emails to all and sundry.
Finally, the last straw came when he began circulating probate documents
containing financial information relative to the wife’s grandparents’ estates
to prominent members of the Jewish community, parents of children attending his
daughters’ daycare and school and members of the Asper Campus.

…..

[125]  Since the last order, there has been relative
peace for the children, the wife and her family, although I note that the
husband appears to search the online Court Registry and Companies Branch
documents regularly in his quest for information about people with whom he has
an issue.  In argument, he defended his prying into people’s lives as
justified, claiming that “knowledge is power.”

[126]  The wife seeks to continue the order with small
variations and the husband asks the court to rescind it in its entirety.
He is particularly concerned with the prohibition from attending near the Asper
Campus.

[127]  Before any prevention order was in place, the
husband was issued a notice under
The
Petty Trespasses Act
, R.S.M. 1987,
c. P50, that he was not welcome on the premises of the Asper Campus.  This
notice was issued after the September 2003 incident in the cafeteria and in
effect, bans the husband from the facility.  This meant he could not visit
the children at the daycare centre or school or participate in any of the
sporting, cultural and social activities of the Campus, the hub of Jewish life
in Winnipeg.

…..

[134]  As far as the
other various provisions of the prevention order are concerned, I determine
that most of them should remain in place, subject to some small
variations.  In my view, the provisions of the other orders have granted
the wife and children some peace and that should continue.  Further, the
husband needs to concentrate on his relationship with his children and as his
unacceptable behaviour toward them has improved while he was under these court
restrictions, it will be to their benefit that he continues to be governed by
them.

[
29
]

The appearance to me is that any improvement
in the conduct, the behavior and the capacity for self-control of the
respondent over time has been modest, as described in the recent evidence of
his daughters and the petitioner, which evidence I find far more persuasive
than that which he has offered.

[
30
]

One of his two children wishes no
contact or communication with him at all. Neither wants him to be free of the
prevention order, which greatly restricts his ability to be near them or to contact
them. The black letter terms of the prevention order appear not to have been
violated by the respondent, since it was varied. But contrary to its spirit,
and to the express wishes of, and requests made to him by, his children, in the
last number of months in particular, he has repeatedly communicated with and
contacted at least his younger daughter in circumstances where she felt
harassed, and feared for her safety. His older daughter, who seems to have
greater resiliency, still expresses fears like her sister.

[
31
]

Having regard to all of the foregoing
circumstances, and to
s. 19(1)
of the
DSVA
, I conclude it is not
fit and just to delete or vary the terms of the prevention order as it relates
to these children, and that it is fit and just that it remain in place. I so
order.

Thomson
J.
